dev.meta_description: Automate course authoring and learner provisioning with the ClassroomHub REST API, Webhooks, and MCP server. Documented, versioned, no integration tax.
dev.subhead: ClassroomHub ships with a public REST API, signed Webhooks, and an MCP server. No closed marketplace, no "premium connector" plans. Build the integration that fits your stack.
dev.api_heading: Everything in the LMS is reachable over HTTP.

0.question: Does hosting a public course cost extra?
0.answer: No. Public courses are part of your existing ClassroomHub workspace. Every paid plan can publish them, and learners do not count against your seat limits until they enroll in a paid course.

1.question: Can I require payment, or capture leads on a public course?
1.answer: Yes. You can attach a payment link, a discount code, or an invite token to the enrollment flow. You can also place callout cards inside lessons that link to a paid course, a community, or any URL you choose.

2.question: Do I need a custom domain?
2.answer: No. Every public course is available on your ClassroomHub public site by default. A custom domain is optional if you want the course to live at your own URL.

3.question: Can search engines index a public course?
3.answer: Yes. Public course landing pages and lesson previews are server-rendered and include the metadata search engines need, so courses are discoverable.

4.question: How are quizzes graded?
4.answer: Instantly in the browser. Public courses support 15 auto-gradable question types, including multiple choice, ordering, matching, hotspot, fill-in-the-blank, numeric, short answer, and file upload.

5.question: Can I gate some lessons and leave the rest public?
5.answer: Yes. Lock the lessons you want to gate and the viewer will show a callout card in place of the content. You can use that card to send people to the paid version of the course.

6.question: Can I match the course page to my brand?
6.answer: Yes. You can choose a landing theme, upload your logo, set a site name, and optionally connect a custom domain. Dark mode is built in for learners.

0.title: Use documentation when the reader knows what they need.
0.description: Docs are best for lookup, reference, troubleshooting, API details, product behavior, release notes, and anything a user needs to search in the moment.

1.title: Use a company academy when the learner needs a guided path.
1.description: Academies are best when people need onboarding, role-based training, practice, proof of completion, certification, or a repeatable learning journey.

0.note: The person already has a task in mind and needs the fastest reliable answer.

1.note: Beginners need sequencing, context, examples, and a clear path from first step to confident use.

2.note: Expertise needs assessment, completion records, certificates, or some visible proof of readiness.

3.note: Partner onboarding usually needs role-based paths, assignments, progress tracking, and certification.

4.note: Lookup work should stay searchable, skimmable, linkable, and easy to update.

5.note: Completion, reminders, renewals, and audit evidence belong in an academy or LMS.

6.note: API details, parameters, edge cases, and error codes work best as documentation.

7.note: A program needs structure: lessons, cohorts or audiences, assessments, certificates, and analytics.

docsUseCases.0: Product setup steps that users need to revisit
docsUseCases.1: API references, SDK details, Webhooks, limits, and errors
docsUseCases.3: Troubleshooting articles and known issue workarounds
docsUseCases.4: Release notes, migration notes, and changelogs
docsUseCases.5: Short answers that support, success, and sales teams repeatedly send

academyUseCases.0: New employee, customer, or partner onboarding
academyUseCases.1: Admin training for complex products or internal systems
academyUseCases.2: Certification for resellers, agencies, consultants, or power users
academyUseCases.3: Compliance training that needs proof, renewal, and audit evidence
academyUseCases.4: Feature adoption programs after a major product launch
academyUseCases.5: Role-based enablement for sales, support, implementation, or customer success teams

0.title: If the audience is searching, write docs.
0.description: Search intent usually means the person already has context. They need precision, not a course. Make the page easy to scan, link related topics, and keep it current.

1.title: If the audience needs sequence, build an academy.
1.description: Sequence matters when concepts depend on each other. A company academy can start with foundations, add practice, check understanding, then issue proof.

2.title: If the business needs proof, build an academy.
2.description: Docs can inform, but they rarely prove readiness. Use courses, assessments, completion records, and certificates when managers need to know who is trained.

3.title: If different roles need different outcomes, build paths.
3.description: A support agent, admin, reseller, and executive sponsor should not read the same long documentation tree. Academies let each role follow a purpose-built path.

0.title: Docs stay as the source of truth
0.description: Keep canonical facts in documentation: product behavior, technical references, setup options, screenshots, limitations, and troubleshooting details.

1.title: Academy packages the learning journey
1.description: Turn the most important docs into guided lessons with context, order, exercises, quizzes, examples, and certificates.

2.title: Support and success route people to the right layer
2.description: Send advanced users to docs for quick answers. Send new users, partners, and internal teams to academy paths when they need structured training.

academySignals.0: People keep asking for onboarding calls even though docs exist.
academySignals.1: Customers read the docs but still do not adopt the full workflow.
academySignals.2: Managers ask who has completed training.
academySignals.3: Partners need certification before they sell or implement.
academySignals.4: Compliance, policy, or process training needs renewal evidence.
academySignals.5: Product changes require more than an announcement.

docs_vs_academy.most_teams_do_not_need_to: Most teams do not need to choose one forever. They need to understand the job each format performs. This guide explains when docs are enough, when a company academy is the better tool, and how the two should work together.
docs_vs_academy.start_with_the_need_then_choose: Start with the need, then choose the format.
docs_vs_academy.if_the_person_wants_one_answer: If the person wants one answer, documentation is usually right. If the person needs a path, proof, or repeatable onboarding, a company academy is usually right.
docs_vs_academy.choose_documentation_when_the_task_is: Choose documentation when the task is searchable, narrow, and repeatable.
docs_vs_academy.documentation_works_best_when_the_user: Documentation works best when the user has a specific job and needs a precise answer. Easy to find, easy to scan, easy to trust — no enrollment required.
docs_vs_academy.choose_a_company_academy_when_capability: Choose a company academy when capability, behavior change, or proof matters.
docs_vs_academy.an_academy_turns_scattered_knowledge_int: An academy turns scattered knowledge into a structured path. Use it when the learner needs context before details, practice before independence, or a certificate before being trusted with a role.
docs_vs_academy.the_strongest_teams_use_docs_and: The strongest teams use docs and academies together.
docs_vs_academy.treat_documentation_as_the_reference_lay: Treat documentation as the reference layer and the academy as the enablement layer. The academy should not duplicate every page in your docs. It should organize the important material into an outcome-driven path.
docs_vs_academy.a_practical_guide_to_when_your: A practical guide to when your company needs documentation, when it needs a company academy, and how both work together for onboarding, enablement, and certification.

0.name: Intercom Articles
0.good: Best-in-class in-app help widget. Great search. Where short-form, "right-now" answers belong.
0.missing: No sequenced learning paths. No assessments. No certification. No per-learner progress.

1.name: Zendesk Guide
1.good: Mature knowledge base, deeply integrated with Zendesk tickets. Excellent for tier-1 deflection.
1.missing: No course structure, no grading, no certificates. Built for support, not for learning.

2.name: Confluence
2.good: The default internal docs tool. Cheap, ubiquitous, easy to write into.
2.missing: Not customer-facing by default. No course primitives. No public certs. No learner analytics.

0.title: Keep your help docs.
0.body: When a customer already knows what they need, they search. Help docs win at lookup. Don't rip out the tool that already does that job well.

1.title: Add a customer academy alongside.
1.body: When a customer needs to learn the product (onboarding, role-based programs, certification, adoption courses for new features), that's the job an academy was built for.
